anchor_text: Being mechanical, you ought not walk
summary: 'Mechanical' here means a manual laborer or craftsman -- someone who works with their hands for wages. Flavius is asserting that tradespeople were legally required to wear their work clothes and carry their tools in public on working days so their social rank would be visible.

Flavius's challenge -- 'where is thy leather apron and thy rule?' -- is the practical enforcement of that rule. The word 'mechanical' carried a class sneer in Elizabethan English; compare 'hempen homespuns' and 'rude mechanicals' in A Midsummer Night's Dream 3.1.

anchor_text: we make holiday to see Caesar and to rejoice in his triumph
summary: A Roman triumph was a formal military parade through Rome, awarded by the Senate only for a war against a foreign enemy in which at least 5,000 enemy soldiers were killed. The general rode in a special chariot, preceded by captive prisoners in chains, and the crowds lined the streets to celebrate. Caesar's triumph here is over Pompey's sons in Spain (45 BC), which made his triumph deeply controversial -- see the note on 'Pompey's blood' below.

The Roman rules technically prohibited a triumph for a civil war -- enemies had to be foreign -- so the tribunes' anger is grounded in Roman law and custom. Shakespeare follows Plutarch closely in making the plebeians' holiday-making the trigger for the tribunes' protest.

anchor_text: Knew you not Pompey? Many a time and oft Have you climb'd up to walls and battlements

anchor_text: That comes in triumph over Pompey's blood
summary: 'Pompey's blood' means Pompey's sons and his surviving supporters -- 'blood' is used in the sense of bloodline or family. Shakespeare compresses the historical timeline: Pompey himself had been dead since 48 BC, but his sons were still fighting in 45 BC.

anchor_text: Pray to the gods to intermit the plague That needs must light on this ingratitude
summary: 'Intermit' means to hold back or suspend -- Marullus asks the people to pray that the gods withhold the plague that must, he says, inevitably punish such ingratitude. anchor_text: These growing feathers pluck'd from Caesar's wing Will make him fly an ordinary pitch
summary: Flavius uses an extended falconry metaphor to close the scene. 'Pitch' is the height a trained hawk reaches before stooping (diving) at prey; 'an ordinary pitch' means a normal, manageable height. Flavius is saying that by removing popular enthusiasm (the 'feathers'), they will keep Caesar at a level where he cannot soar beyond the control of other citizens.
detail: Falconry was the prestige sport of the Elizabethan aristocracy, and its vocabulary -- pitch, stoop, tower, haggard, wing -- was widely understood. 'Pluck feathers from a wing' to reduce a bird's flight was a real falconry technique. The metaphor does double political work: it frames Caesar as a trained bird of prey who has grown dangerously wild, and frames the tribunes' task as keepers restoring order. The image recurs in Shakespeare's political plays: compare 'tower' in Richard II and the 'eagle' imagery in Hamlet and Cymbeline.

anchor_text: touched in this holy chase, Shake off their sterile curse
summary: The Lupercalia was a Roman fertility festival held on 15 February. anchor_text: Beware the Ides of March
summary: The 'Ides' were a mid-month marker in the Roman calendar: the 15th in March, May, July, and October, the 13th in all other months. 'Beware the Ides of March' means 'watch out for 15 March' -- the day Caesar will be assassinated at the Capitol.

Plutarch records that a soothsayer named Spurinna warned Caesar in advance to 'take heed of the day of the Ides of March.' (North trans., 'Life of Caesar.') The warning was so famous in antiquity that it became proverbial; Shakespeare takes it directly from Plutarch.

summary: Brutus holds the office of praetor -- a senior Roman magistrate just below consul, roughly equivalent to a chief judge. Cassius is planting forged letters in Brutus's official chair, his home window, and on the statue of Lucius Junius Brutus -- the legendary ancestor who expelled Rome's last king. The forgeries are designed to make Brutus think ordinary Romans are begging him to act against Caesar, just as his ancestor acted against Tarquin.

Placing a document in it was a formal public gesture, as if the Roman people were petitioning their magistrate. Shakespeare follows Plutarch closely here, but makes Cassius the forger rather than anonymous citizens.

anchor_text: His countenance, like richest alchemy, Will change to virtue and to worthiness
summary: Casca is comparing Brutus's public authority to alchemy -- the medieval and Renaissance attempt to transmute base metals into gold. His point is that the same action that would look like criminal murder if Cassius or Casca did it will be transformed into honorable virtue simply because Brutus is involved. Brutus's personal reputation is the 'philosopher's stone' that turns lead into gold.
detail: Alchemy was not merely a metaphor for Shakespeare's audience; it was a recognized (if controversial) proto-science with serious royal and noble patrons in Elizabethan England. The word 'countenance' carries both 'face/appearance' and 'support/approval' -- both meanings apply: Brutus's very presence and his endorsement will legitimize the conspiracy. This is one of the play's most compressed statements of its central political problem: that the conspiracy's public meaning depends entirely on Brutus's moral reputation rather than on the intrinsic justice of the act.

anchor_text: the bright day that brings forth the adder
summary: Brutus constructs his case against Caesar by analogy: just as warm sunshine rouses a venomous snake from its hiding place, political power and a crown would draw out a dangerous ambition that may currently lie dormant in Caesar. The image illustrates his logic that the risk is not who Caesar is now but what he would become.
detail: The argument is a hypothetical-conditional syllogism: crowning Caesar is like warming the ground that wakes the adder. Brutus himself concedes he has never seen Caesar's reason overborne by passion -- he is arguing from possibility, not evidence. Critics from Coleridge onward have noted this as the logical flaw at the heart of Brutus's decision: he reasons from what a man might do, not from what the man has done. See Plutarch, 'Life of Brutus' (North 1579): 'Brutus would never consent to the death of Caesar for any private quarrel, but only for the common benefit of the people.'

anchor_text: My ancestors did from the streets of Rome The Tarquin drive
summary: Brutus invokes his legendary ancestor Lucius Junius Brutus, who in 509 BC led the revolt that expelled Tarquinius Superbus ('Tarquin the Proud'), Rome's last king, and founded the Roman Republic. For Marcus Brutus, this ancestry is both an inspiration and an obligation: his family name is synonymous with the end of kingship.

anchor_text: Between the acting of a dreadful thing And the first motion, all the interim is Like a phantasma or a hideous dream
summary: Brutus describes the psychological torment of having decided to do something terrible but not yet having done it. 'Phantasma' (TLN 630) means hallucination or waking nightmare. He compares his inner state to a small kingdom in civil war: the rational soul ('genius') and the bodily faculties ('mortal instruments') are at war, just as a government is paralyzed by insurrection.

'Genius' in Roman belief was a man's personal guardian spirit, the divine element that animates and guides him; Shakespeare uses the term precisely in its Roman sense. 'Mortal instruments' are the physical powers of the body (hands, limbs) that must execute what the mind commands. The metaphor of the self as a miniature state ('little kingdom') is a commonplace of Renaissance political thought, but Brutus's use of it here is psychologically acute: the 'insurrection' in his soul is a civil war, directly mirroring the political plot being hatched.

anchor_text: Not Erebus itself were dim enough To hide thee from prevention
summary: Erebus is the primordial darkness of the underworld in Greek mythology -- deeper and more absolute than night. Brutus is saying that if conspiracy went openly in the world, there would be no darkness dark enough to conceal it; even the blackest depth of Hades could not hide it from discovery and suppression ('prevention' = being caught before you can act).
detail: In Hesiod's Theogony (123), Erebus is one of the first beings to emerge from Chaos, a personification of deep darkness before the gods take shape. The name passed into Latin poetry (Virgil, Aeneid 4.26; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.76) as a synonym for the underworld's darkest region. Brutus's use is rhetorically extravagant -- hyperbole designed to underscore the moral ugliness of conspiracy that must hide even at night.

anchor_text: No, not an oath: if not the face of men
summary: Brutus rejects Cassius's suggestion that the conspirators swear an oath to bind themselves together. anchor_text: his silver hairs Will purchase us a good opinion
summary: Metellus Cimber wants to recruit Cicero because Cicero's age and enormous reputation as a statesman and orator would give the conspiracy an air of legitimate gravitas. anchor_text: Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius
summary: Brutus insists the conspirators kill Caesar as a ritual sacrifice -- a formal, purposeful killing in service of Rome -- rather than as butchers driven by personal hatred or revenge. He extends the metaphor: Caesar should be 'carved' like a dish fit for the gods, not hacked like meat for hounds. This language frames the assassination as a religious or civic act, not murder.
detail: Roman sacrifice (Latin: sacrificium) was a public, formal rite in which an animal was killed in an officially sanctioned way to propitiate the gods. The sacrificer (sacerdos or pontifex) used precise ritual cuts; a botched sacrifice was an ill omen. By claiming the role of sacrificer, Brutus is positioning the killing as lawful and holy. The dramatic irony is that the play will immediately undercut this framing: Antony's funeral speech turns the bloodied body into evidence of murder, not sacrifice. Note also that Brutus here overrides Cassius's practical judgment that Antony must also die -- a decision that proves fatal to the conspiracy.

anchor_text: Peace! count the clock. The clock hath stricken three.
summary: Mechanical striking clocks did not exist in ancient Rome; they were invented in medieval Europe around the 13th century. Shakespeare places an anachronistic striking clock in the scene. It is one of several such anachronisms in the play -- Caesar's doublet (3.1), for example -- that scholars have discussed at length without resolution.

Ben Jonson mocked Shakespeare for careless errors of this kind. However, some critics argue Shakespeare was indifferent to historical costume and deliberately blended ancient Rome with the look of Elizabethan England because his stage had no other vocabulary for depicting a powerful, civilized, republican city-state. The anachronism does not disturb an Elizabethan audience because the Globe stage made no attempt at Roman costuming. See E.K. Chambers, William Shakespeare: A Study of Facts and Problems (1930), vol. 1.

summary: Roman augurers (augures) were priests who read divine will through the flight patterns of birds, the behavior of sacred chickens, lightning, and other signs. Plutarch records that on the morning of the assassination a haruspex (a specialist in reading entrails) sacrificed an animal and found no heart -- a dire omen Caesar dismissed. See Plutarch, 'Life of Caesar' (North 1579). The play's reference to Caesar being 'superstitious grown' (TLN 771) is consistent with Plutarch's account of his growing trust in diviners near the end of his life, a change from his earlier skepticism.

anchor_text: is it physical To walk unbraced and suck up the humours Of the dank morning
summary: Portia uses the medical language of her day: 'physical' means medicinal or good for your health (the opposite of its modern sense). 'Humours' refers to the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that Elizabethan medicine believed controlled health and temperament. 'Suck up the humours of the dank morning' means breathing in the damp morning air, which was thought to carry bad humours that could make you ill. 'Unbraced' means with your doublet unlaced and open.
detail: Galenic humoral medicine, dominant in Europe from antiquity through the 17th century, held that disease resulted from an imbalance of the four humours. 'Dank' (cold and damp) morning air was specifically associated with phlegm and melancholy, and medical handbooks warned against exposure before sunrise. Portia's sarcasm is medical as well as emotional: Brutus is prescribing rest for himself while simultaneously doing everything a physician would forbid. See Galen's doctrine as summarized in Thomas Elyot, The Castel of Helth (1539), ch. 1.

anchor_text: Dwell I but in the suburbs Of your good pleasure? If it be no more, Portia is Brutus' harlot, not his wife.
summary: Portia uses a sharp geographic metaphor: London's (and Rome's) brothels and houses of prostitution were legally confined to the suburbs outside the city walls. To 'dwell in the suburbs' of a husband's pleasure is to occupy only the marginal, commercial part of his affections -- the role of a paid mistress ('harlot'), not a true wife. She is demanding the full rights of a Roman wife, not a concubine.
detail: In Elizabethan London, the Southwark stews (brothels) lay just outside the city proper, across the Thames -- geographically 'suburban.' The same spatial logic applied to ancient Rome, where prostitution was regulated to specific districts. Portia's argument draws on the Roman legal concept of the Roman matron (matrona) whose dignity and honor were distinct from those of a courtesan: a wife had a legal right to her husband's confidences within the institution of marriage. Her speech anticipates her self-wounding at TLN 877-879, which is her proof that she deserves to be trusted as a full partner.

anchor_text: O constancy, be strong upon my side
summary: Portia is invoking 'constancy' as a virtue -- the Stoic quality of mental firmness and self-control under pressure. She is asking her own resolve not to crack and betray what she knows about the conspiracy.
detail: In Stoic philosophy, which shaped Roman aristocratic self-presentation and pervades this play, 'constancy' (Latin constantia) was one of the highest virtues: the ability to keep one's passions from overriding one's reason. Portia, daughter of the Stoic Cato and wife of the Stoic Brutus, holds herself to that standard. Her appeal to it here reveals how much she has internalized that ethos -- and how near she is to failing it. Plutarch records Portia's famous self-wounding to prove she could endure pain and keep secrets (Plutarch, 'Life of Brutus,' North trans. 1579).

anchor_text: I have a man's mind, but a woman's might
summary: Portia accepts the Roman belief that women have inferior physical and emotional endurance compared to men, while claiming her mind -- her reason and resolution -- is equal to a man's. The word 'might' here means strength or capacity, not power.
detail: Roman ideology, filtered through Stoic philosophy, held that women were governed more by passion and less by reason than men, making them unfit for public life and untrustworthy with secrets. Portia explicitly argues against that conventional view of herself, but accepts its framework: she has the rational mind (male, Stoic), but her body and emotional 'might' are female and therefore weaker. This self-division drives the entire scene. Plutarch praises Portia precisely because she overcame her female 'nature' (Plutarch, 'Life of Brutus,' North 1579). The next line -- 'How hard it is for women to keep counsel' -- makes the anxiety explicit.

anchor_text: How hard it is for women to keep counsel
summary: 'Keep counsel' means to keep a secret, to stay silent about what one knows. Portia fears she will accidentally reveal that she knows about the plot against Caesar.
detail: The phrase 'keep counsel' (also 'hold counsel') was a standard early modern idiom for maintaining secrecy. It appears repeatedly in Shakespeare -- Launce uses it comically in Two Gentlemen of Verona, and it recurs in legal contexts where 'counsel' meant a confidential communication. Here the stakes are lethal: if Portia's knowledge of the conspiracy becomes visible, Brutus dies. Her aside is therefore not just emotional outburst but a near-slip that Lucius might overhear, and she is aware of the danger (line 1115: 'Sure, the boy heard me').

anchor_text: About the ninth hour, lady
summary: Romans divided daylight into twelve equal hours counted from sunrise. The 'ninth hour' therefore falls roughly three-quarters of the way through the day -- about 3 p.m. in summer, or around 2 p.m. in the shorter days of mid-March. The scene is set before Caesar has yet left for the Capitol, placing it in the morning.

In March a Roman 'ninth hour' would be roughly modern 2:30-3:00 p.m. However, stage time in Elizabethan drama compresses historical time freely: this scene runs parallel to Brutus's morning preparations (Act 2 Scene 2), so the 'ninth hour' functions more as a dramatic signal of Caesar still being at home and the day advancing toward catastrophe than as a precisely calculated clock-time. Early editors (Malone and Capell) note this casual handling of Roman time. Cf. Plutarch, 'Life of Caesar,' North 1579, for the morning of the Ides.

anchor_text: Of Senators, of Praetors, common suitors
summary: Praetors were elected Roman magistrates ranking just below consuls -- senior judges and administrators who commanded armies in the provinces. Brutus and Cassius both held the praetorship, which is part of why they could stand close enough to Caesar to strike him. 'Common suitors' are ordinary petitioners seeking Caesar's favor.
detail: By 44 BCE the praetorship was one of the key rungs on the cursus honorum, the Roman career ladder. Caesar had appointed or confirmed many of the praetors himself, including Brutus (praetor urbanus, the most senior of the eight), which made the conspirators' access to him that day unremarkable. Artemidorus names the crowd pressing Caesar precisely because their closeness was the assassins' weapon and their cover: ordinary petitioners mixed with the conspirators in the same press. Plutarch, 'Life of Caesar,' North 1579, describes the crowd around Caesar on the Ides.

The definition of praetors and the specific identification of Brutus as praetor urbanus are historically accurate and relevant; the observation that their office gave conspirators unremarkable proximity to Caesar is a sound, well-documented historical inference without overreach.

anchor_text: The Ides of March are come
summary: The 'Ides of March' is the Roman calendar term for March 15. Caesar's line echoes the soothsayer's earlier warning (1.2), and the Soothsayer's reply -- 'but not gone' -- reminds the audience that the danger is still present. Caesar's casual tone shows he believes he has outlasted the prophecy.
detail: The Roman calendar divided each month by three fixed points: the Kalends (1st), the Nones (5th or 7th), and the Ides (13th or 15th, depending on the month). March, May, July, and October had their Ides on the 15th; all other months on the 13th. The Ides were sacred to Jupiter. The assassination on this day was historically confirmed by Plutarch, Suetonius, and Cicero's letters. Plutarch, 'Life of Julius Caesar,' in North's translation (1579), records the soothsayer's original warning.

anchor_text: What touches us ourself shall be last served
summary: Caesar speaks of himself in the royal 'we' ('us ourself'), a habit Shakespeare gives him to signal his self-aggrandizement. He is also applying a Roman aristocratic principle: a great man's private business yields to public duties. The irony is that Artemidorus's letter would save his life, yet Caesar waves it aside as a personal matter.
detail: The use of 'we' / 'us' for a single speaker (the 'royal plural' or 'majestic plural') was associated in Elizabethan England with the sovereign's formal voice. Shakespeare gives Caesar this construction repeatedly to dramatize his claim to near-divine status. Plutarch, 'Life of Caesar' (North, 1579), describes Caesar receiving petitions at the Capitol; Shakespeare invents the detail of Artemidorus's letter and Caesar's refusal to read it first.

anchor_text: These couchings and these lowly courtesies
summary: 'Couchings' means prostrations -- lying flat or kneeling to the ground in submission. Caesar is dismissing the whole ritual of flattering petition: bowing, kneeling, and what he calls 'base spaniel-fawning' (a spaniel was the symbol of a cringing, slavish dog). His point is that no degree of theatrical humility will change a decree he has already made by reason.
detail: In Roman senatorial practice, petitioners would kneel or even prostrate themselves before a magistrate of superior power. Caesar's refusal to be moved by this is framed as a mark of his constancy and rational superiority, but his language also reveals his contempt for the men around him. 'Spaniel-fawning' draws on the Elizabethan stereotype of the spaniel as an obsequiously affectionate dog; cf. Onions, 'A Shakespeare Glossary,' s.v. 'spaniel' (fawning, servile creature). The passage anticipates his 'northern star' self-comparison two speeches later.

anchor_text: turn pre-ordinance and first decree / Into the law of children
summary: 'Pre-ordinance' means a law established beforehand by deliberate decree, not improvised in the heat of emotion. Caesar is saying that to change an established ruling because someone kneels and begs would reduce serious law to something as arbitrary and childish as a child's caprice -- promises that change with whim. It is a claim that his word, once given, is permanent.

anchor_text: I am constant as the northern star
summary: Caesar compares himself to the North Star (Polaris), the only star whose position in the sky does not appear to shift as the Earth rotates. Every other star moves; Polaris alone 'holds its place.' The extended comparison -- stars in the sky are like men on earth, and he alone is the fixed one -- is the rhetorical device of an extended metaphor (or conceit). The speech is meant to justify refusing Metellus Cimber's petition, but its grandiosity also shows Caesar's fatal arrogance moments before the knives appear.
detail: The speech runs TLN 1187-1200 and is one of Shakespeare's most elaborate self-comparisons. The metaphor works on two levels: cosmological (the fixed star among moving ones) and political (the one constant man in a world of wavering flesh). 'Apprehensive' (TLN 1194) means capable of feeling and fear -- a quality Caesar claims to have transcended. Plutarch does not record this speech; it is Shakespeare's invention to dramatize Caesar's hubris. The rhetorical term for a sustained metaphor elaborated in detail is an 'extended conceit' or 'conceit' (from the Italian concetto, concept); cf. Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon,' s.v. 'conceit.'

anchor_text: wilt thou lift up Olympus
summary: Mount Olympus (in northern Greece) was in Greek and Roman mythology the home of the gods -- a place no mortal could reach or move. Caesar's retort to Cinna -- 'Will you try to lift up Mount Olympus?' -- is a contemptuous comparison: trying to change Caesar's mind is as futile as trying to physically move the home of the gods. It is his final speech before the assassins strike.

anchor_text: Et tu, Brute?
summary: 'Et tu, Brute?' is Latin for 'And you, Brutus?' or 'Even you, Brutus?' It is Caesar's last utterance upon seeing Brutus among the assassins -- the one man whose blow he did not expect. The phrase is Shakespeare's invention; Latin sources record a Greek phrase (attributed by Suetonius) or silence. The words have become the defining expression in English for the shock of betrayal by someone trusted.

Plutarch ('Life of Caesar,' North 1579, p. 793) says Caesar pulled his toga over his face and fell without words. Shakespeare probably knew Suetonius through Golding or directly in Latin. He converts the Greek into Latin to signal historical dignity and to make the moment legible for an Elizabethan audience who had studied Latin at school. The phrase had appeared in the earlier play 'Caesar's Revenge' (c. 1594) and was already familiar on the English stage.

anchor_text: How many ages hence / Shall this our lofty scene be acted o'er / In States unborn and accents yet unknown
summary: Cassius and Brutus imagine future generations performing this very scene on stage -- a moment of self-conscious theatricality (called 'metatheatre') in which the characters seem to know they are in a famous story. 'Accents yet unknown' means languages not yet in existence. Shakespeare was writing for audiences who were, in fact, one of those future peoples, which gives the lines a quiet irony: the play you are watching is the 'acted o'er' that Cassius predicts.

By having Cassius and Brutus claim the dignity of being historical exempla -- models for future actors -- Shakespeare simultaneously elevates the conspirators and undercuts them: they are bragging about their fame at the moment their enterprise is already doomed. The 'Pompey's basis' reference (TLN 1247) locates Caesar's body at the foot of Pompey's statue, a detail from Plutarch ('Life of Caesar,' North 1579, p. 792) and historically confirmed by Suetonius. anchor_text: on Pompey's basis lies along

Plutarch, 'Life of Julius Caesar' (North 1579, p. 792), records that 'he fell down at the foot of the pedestal whereon Pompey's image stood.' anchor_text: Here wast thou bay'd, brave hart; / Here didst thou fall; and here thy hunters stand, / Sign'd in thy spoil
summary: Antony sustains a hunting pun across three lines: Caesar is a 'hart' (a male deer, homophone of 'heart'), 'bay'd' (cornered by dogs, as in a stag hunt), and his killers are 'hunters' 'sign'd in thy spoil' (marked with the deer's blood, as hunters were after the kill). The line 'O world, thou wast the forest to this hart / And this, indeed, O world, the heart of thee' then shifts the pun: Caesar was both the 'hart' hunted through the world (Rome) and the 'heart' -- the center and core -- of it. The wordplay works because 'hart' and 'heart' were near-homophones in Elizabethan English.
detail: The stag-hunt was the most prestigious form of aristocratic hunting in both ancient Rome and Elizabethan England. After the kill, hunters would smear themselves with the deer's blood -- a ritual called 'taking the grease' -- as a mark of honor. Antony applies this image to the conspirators' blood-stained hands and swords. The 'hart/heart' pun was a recognized Elizabethan wordplay; cf. Schmidt, 'Shakespeare-Lexicon,' s.v. 'hart' and 'heart.' Plutarch does not record this speech; Shakespeare invented it for Antony. The sustained hunting metaphor is a 'conceit' -- an extended metaphorical figure developed across multiple lines.

anchor_text: Of your philosophy you make no use, If you give place to accidental evils

anchor_text: There is a tide in the affairs of men Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; Omitted, all the voyage of their life Is bound in shallows and in miseries

anchor_text: cold demeanor in Octavius' wing
summary: 'Cold demeanor' means sluggish, unenthusiastic fighting behavior. Brutus has spotted that Octavius's flank of the enemy army seems reluctant or hesitant, and he means to exploit that weakness before it stiffens.

anchor_text: In Parthia did I take thee prisoner
summary: Parthia was a powerful empire east of Rome, roughly modern-day Iran and Iraq. Roman campaigns against Parthia were frequent and often disastrous; the most famous defeat was Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC). Cassius served in that campaign as quaestor and actually rescued some survivors. Pindarus, taken as a prisoner of war there, became Cassius's slave.
detail: In 53 BC Marcus Licinius Crassus led a Roman army into Parthia and was annihilated at the Battle of Carrhae. Cassius, serving as quaestor, managed to lead remnants of the army to safety. Plutarch records this as a mark of Cassius's military competence: 'Life of Crassus,' chs. 25-31; 'Life of Brutus,' ch. 12. The detail that Pindarus was a Parthian captive is Shakespeare's invention or inference, but it grounds the oath of absolute obedience in a historically plausible military transaction.

anchor_text: Now be a freeman; and with this good sword, That ran through Caesar's bowels
summary: Cassius offers Pindarus his legal freedom (manumission) in exchange for killing him. Roman law required a formal act to free a slave; Cassius's word here is a deathbed grant of liberty. The detail that this is the same sword used to stab Caesar ties the death of Cassius back to the assassination, suggesting Caesar's ghost is taking its revenge through that weapon.
detail: Roman manumission could be informal (per mensam, by the master's declaration before witnesses) or formal (vindicta, before a magistrate). Cassius's battlefield declaration is the informal type but would have been legally binding under Roman custom. Pindarus's flight 'far from this country' after the deed (TLN 2399-2400) suggests he does not trust that freedom to hold now that his master is dead and Rome is in the hands of the Triumvirs. The sword that 'ran through Caesar's bowels' makes the instrument of the assassination the literal instrument of Cassius's death, a symmetry that fulfills Brutus's later line about Caesar's spirit turning the conspirators' swords in their own entrails (TLN 2449-2450).

anchor_text: Caesar, thou art revenged, Even with the sword that kill'd thee.
summary: Cassius addresses the dead Caesar directly, acknowledging that Caesar is being avenged by the very weapon that killed him. This is the first of a series of moments in Act 5 in which the conspirators recognize that Caesar's spirit is undoing them. Cassius, who organized the assassination, dies on the assassination's own sword.

The motif runs through the Act: Brutus at TLN 2448-2450 will generalize it ('Thy spirit walks abroad, and turns our swords / In our own proper entrails'), and the Ghost of Caesar appearing to Brutus before the battle (4.3) prepared the audience for this pattern. The phrase 'even with' means 'precisely by means of' or 'exactly through.'

anchor_text: O hateful Error, Melancholy's child! Why dost thou show to the apt thoughts of men The things that are not?
summary: Messala personifies Error as the child of Melancholy -- a psychological theory drawn from Renaissance humoral medicine, which held that people dominated by black bile (melancholics) were prone to misreading reality, seeing threats and disasters that did not exist. 'Things that are not' refers specifically to Pindarus's false report that Titinius was captured.
detail: Elizabethan humoral theory (derived from Galen via Levinus Lemnius and Timothy Bright) held that the melancholic humor distorted perception and induced morbid visions. Cassius himself had earlier been described as having 'a lean and hungry look' (1.2) and seeing things that are not: 'he is a great observer, and he looks quite through the deeds of men' (1.2). Messala's apostrophe to Error, cast as the offspring of Melancholy, frames the catastrophe as psychologically determined -- Cassius's constitutional pessimism (melancholy) produced a misreading (error) that killed him. The extended metaphor of Error as a child who kills its own mother ('kill'st the mother that engender'd thee') is an example of adynaton used as moral irony: misreading produces a result that destroys its own cause.

sources.name: Bright

The humoral reading of Melancholy producing misperception is a mainstream early-modern framework, the verbal logic ('Error ... kill'st the mother that engender'd thee') is correctly identified as moral irony, and the connection to Cassius's earlier characterisation in 1.2 is textually defensible; the label 'adynaton' is slightly imprecise (the figure is closer to paradox or irony), but this does not undermine the interpretation.

anchor_text: By your leave, gods: this is a Roman's part
summary: 'A Roman's part' means the proper duty of a Roman: to die by one's own hand rather than be captured or survive in dishonor. Titinius asks the gods' permission before taking his own life -- a Roman gesture acknowledging that suicide requires divine sanction even while asserting it as a civic duty. This is the Stoic-Roman ideal of honorable self-killing.
detail: The phrase 'by your leave, gods' registers the theological complexity of Roman suicide: the act required justification even in a culture that valued it. Cicero's Tusculan Disputations (I.30) and Plato's Phaedo (which Brutus would have read) both treat the conditions under which self-killing is permissible. Cato the Younger's suicide (46 BC), the model for all later Republican suicides in this play, was accompanied by deliberate philosophical preparation. Titinius's brief apology to the gods compresses this tradition into a single line.

The reading of 'a Roman's part' as the Stoic-Roman duty of honourable self-killing is mainstream and well-supported by context; the brief apology to the gods is correctly glossed as acknowledging the theological weight of the act without anachronistic moralising.

anchor_text: O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet! Thy spirit walks abroad, and turns our swords In our own proper entrails.
summary: Brutus acknowledges that Caesar's ghost is still at work, causing the conspirators to die by their own weapons. 'Walks abroad' means 'moves freely through the world.' 'Our own proper entrails' means 'our very own guts' -- 'proper' here is an intensifier, not a compliment. This fulfills the Ghost's promise to meet Brutus 'at Philippi' (4.3).
detail: The idea that a murdered man's spirit could compel the living to destroy themselves was standard in both Greek tragedy (the Erinyes/Furies) and Roman tradition. Plutarch does not give Brutus this speech; Shakespeare adds it to make Brutus himself articulate the theological pattern. 'Walks abroad' echoes the language of classical shades who cannot rest in Hades until avenged -- compare Virgil, Aeneid VI, on unburied souls wandering the banks of the Styx. The Caesar who was physically killed at the Capitol has become metaphysically unkillable.

The interpretation that Brutus consciously articulates the pattern of Caesarian revenge is fully warranted by the text and by the play's established Ghost-of-Caesar motif; the Virgil parallel is offered as illustrative rather than as a direct source claim, which is appropriately cautious.

anchor_text: The last of all the Romans, fare thee well! It is impossible that ever Rome Should breed thy fellow.
summary: Brutus's eulogy declares Cassius uniquely irreplaceable -- 'the last of all the Romans' in the tradition of civic virtue and republican courage. The phrase does not mean Cassius was the last Roman alive, but the last of a type: the incorruptible republican soldier. This is the highest compliment one Roman could pay another in the play's value system.
detail: Plutarch praises Cassius's vigor and military skill but does not record Brutus delivering this exact eulogy. Shakespeare draws on Plutarch's general characterization of the republican cause as ending with these deaths. 'Breed thy fellow' means 'produce your equal.' The eulogy is also ironic: Brutus himself is shortly to demonstrate the same antique Roman virtue by dying on his own sword, making his tribute to Cassius a covert farewell to himself.

The gloss that 'last of all the Romans' means the last exemplar of a republican type rather than the last Roman alive is the correct and mainstream reading; the note that the eulogy is covertly self-referential for Brutus is a defensible and standard scholarly observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: to Thassos send his body: His funerals shall not be in our camp, Lest it discomfort us.
summary: Thassos (modern Thasos) is a Greek island in the northern Aegean Sea, close to Philippi. Brutus orders the body sent there rather than buried on the battlefield, fearing that a funeral within the camp would demoralize the troops before the second engagement. Roman commanders regularly deferred or displaced the burial of important men during active campaigns for exactly this reason.
detail: Plutarch confirms this detail: 'Brutus caused the body of Cassius to be carried to the isle of Thasos, fearing that his funerals within his camp should be an ill sign.' North's translation, 'Life of Brutus,' ch. 43. 'Discomfort' (TLN 2461) means 'discourage, unnerve' -- not a modern sense of mild inconvenience but an older sense of military demoralization. The decision also leaves the stage clear: no Roman funeral rites are shown, which prevents the scene from becoming a reprise of Caesar's funeral in Act 3 and keeps the momentum toward the second battle.

anchor_text: What bastard doth not

By proclaiming his own name in the same breath, Young Cato frames his challenge as a test of courage and noble identity: any man who does not follow him forward is implicitly 'base-born' in spirit regardless of his birth.

anchor_text: I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho
summary: Marcus Cato (Cato the Younger, 95-46 BCE) was the most celebrated Stoic republican of his age. He died by suicide at Utica rather than submit to Julius Caesar, making his name synonymous with uncompromising liberty and principled resistance to tyranny. Young Cato shouts this lineage to announce his cause as much as his identity.
detail: Cato the Younger was the great-grandson of Cato the Censor and served as a tribune and senator who opposed Caesar's ambitions at every turn. After Caesar's victory at Thapsus in 46 BCE, Cato killed himself at Utica in North Africa rather than accept a pardon from the man he considered a tyrant. Plutarch devotes a full Life to Cato Minor, and Shakespeare's audience would have known the name as shorthand for Stoic republican virtue. Portia is Cato's daughter and Brutus's wife, making Young Cato Brutus's brother-in-law; his cry is thus also a claim on the same ideological tradition that motivates Brutus himself. By proclaiming 'a foe to tyrants' in the same breath, Young Cato translates his father's philosophical stance into a battlefield identity.

All historical claims are accurate: Cato's suicide at Utica rather than submit to Caesar, his role as the defining Stoic republican, Portia's parentage making Young Cato Brutus's brother-in-law, and the audience's ready familiarity with the name as shorthand for principled anti-tyranny — all are mainstream and well-sourced in Plutarch via North.

anchor_text: thou diest as bravely as Titinius; And mayst be honour'd, being Cato's son

The comparison also reinforces that to die fighting or by one's own hand was considered honourable in the Roman tradition, while capture was shameful.

anchor_text: Only I yield to die: There is so much that thou wilt kill me straight
summary: Lucilius speaks a deliberate paradox: 'I yield' normally means 'I surrender,' but he qualifies it to mean 'I surrender only to death — not to captivity.' The next line explains: he offers the soldier money ('There is so much') as payment to be killed on the spot, not taken prisoner. He is pretending to be Brutus to draw attention away from the real Brutus.

The phrase 'There is so much' accompanied by the stage direction 'Offering money' means Lucilius is literally paying the soldier to kill him. The rhetorical effect is a compressed riddle: a surrender that is actually a request for execution. This audacious act of loyalty, impersonating Brutus to let the real Brutus escape, is recorded in Plutarch.

anchor_text: Brutus is safe enough: I dare assure thee that no enemy Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus
summary: Lucilius, now unmasked as an impostor, maintains his cover story by stating what he knows to be true as a Roman axiom: the real Brutus would choose death over capture. This doubles as both a pledge of personal loyalty and a statement of Roman honour. Plutarch records this exact incident, making it one of the play's closest borrowings from North's translation.
detail: In Plutarch's 'Life of Brutus' (North, 1579), Lucilius's ruse is recorded in detail: he presented himself as Brutus to the enemy cavalry, was brought to Antony, and told him proudly that Brutus was not taken. Antony's admiring response — keeping Lucilius safe and making him a friend — also follows Plutarch closely. The episode is used in the play to illustrate two ideas simultaneously: the Roman principle that a noble man of integrity is 'like himself' and therefore predictable in choosing death over dishonour; and the counter-intuitive generosity of Antony, who recognises and rewards loyalty even in an enemy. Shakespeare's phrase 'He will be found like Brutus, like himself' (TLN 2491) compresses this into a near-tautology: Brutus's essence and his conduct are identical, because a truly Roman character has no gap between public role and private self.

This also echoes Antony's consistent pattern throughout the play of being drawn to honourable conduct in his opponents.

summary: Statilius was a soldier Brutus sent ahead to check whether the camp was safe; showing a torch was the agreed signal for 'all clear.' His failure to return means he is either captured or dead, confirming the battle is lost.
detail: Plutarch (North 1579, 'Life of Brutus') records that Brutus sent Statilius to scout the enemy camp with instructions to light a torch if he found it safe and then return; the torch was seen but Statilius never came back, having been taken by the enemy. Shakespeare follows this detail closely.

anchor_text: The ghost of Caesar hath appear'd to me Two several times by night; at Sardis once, And this last night here in Philippi fields
summary: Brutus refers to two earlier appearances of Caesar's ghost: once at Sardis in western Turkey while the republican army was marching east, and once the night before this battle. The ghost told Brutus they would meet again 'at Philippi' — a threat that has now come true.

In Roman thinking, an unavenged spirit could haunt its murderer; the ghost functions both as psychological guilt and as a supernatural 'evil spirit' demanding retribution. The fulfilment of the prophecy confirms to Brutus that his death is cosmically inevitable.

anchor_text: our enemies have beat us to the pit: It is more worthy to leap in ourselves Than tarry till they push us
summary: 'The pit' is a hunting trap — a concealed pit dug to catch or kill game — used as a metaphor for inescapable death. Brutus means: the enemy have driven us to the edge of destruction; it is more honorable to jump in voluntarily than to be shoved in as captives.
detail: The pit metaphor extends naturally to the grave and to animal-baiting arenas (where animals were also driven into pits). Shakespeare uses the word in this sense elsewhere, e.g. Hamlet 3.3. The logic is Stoic: self-chosen death at the moment of defeat preserves dignity that surrender destroys. Plutarch records Brutus as saying he would not be led in triumph through Rome ('Life of Brutus,' North 1579).

anchor_text: Thou know'st that we two went to school together; Even for that our love of old, I pr'ythee, Hold thou my sword-hilts
summary: Brutus appeals to a shared boyhood education to ask Volumnius to hold the sword steady while he runs onto it. Volumnius specifically is mentioned as an old comrade from student days in Athens. The mode of death — running onto a held sword — was a recognized form of Roman honorable suicide when no bondman was available to strike the blow, though it was more commonly associated with falling on one's own sword.

anchor_text: I shall have glory by this losing day, More than Octavius and Mark Antony By this vile conquest shall attain unto
summary: Brutus uses a paradox: military defeat will bring him more glory than victory brings his enemies. The argument is that he fought for principle, while Octavius and Antony fight for power — so their 'vile conquest' is morally inferior even though they win. This is a form of the Roman idea that a noble death redeems a lost cause.
detail: The word 'vile' (low, base, ignoble) is doing heavy rhetorical work: Brutus assigns moral worth inversely to military outcome. The claim echoes Stoic philosophy as Cicero articulates it in the Tusculan Disputations: glory comes from virtue, not from success. It also prefigures Antony's eulogy, which grants Brutus the verdict Brutus here predicts. Structurally this speech is Brutus's final self-justification, compressed into three lines.

anchor_text: Night hangs upon mine eyes; my bones would rest That have but labour'd to attain this hour
summary: 'Night hangs upon mine eyes' means darkness is pressing down on his sight — he feels death approaching as a dimming of vision. 'My bones would rest' means his body is exhausted and longs for the stillness of death. Both phrases use physical sensation as a metaphor for dying.
detail: The phrase 'labour'd to attain this hour' is deliberately double: Brutus has worked his whole life, and that labor has led him to this single moment of death. The line can be read as resignation (he is tired), but also as a kind of satisfaction (this is the hour his integrity always demanded). The image of night falling on the eyes recurs in classical descriptions of death; compare Virgil, Aeneid 10.745: 'nox atra caput circumvolat' (black night wheels around the head).

anchor_text: Thou art a fellow of a good respect; Thy life hath had some smack of honor in it
summary: 'A fellow of a good respect' means a man of good reputation or standing. 'Smack' means a taste or trace — Brutus is saying Strato's life has held some genuine flavor of honor. Brutus singles Strato out because he finds him worthy of the task the others refused.

The compliment is carefully calibrated: Brutus does not flatter Strato as a great hero, but acknowledges enough honor in him to trust him with this final service.

anchor_text: Caesar, now be still: I kill'd not thee with half so good a will
summary: Brutus's last words address Caesar's ghost directly. He asks Caesar to be at peace because he is now killing himself with more willingness than he killed Caesar. The rhyming couplet ('still' / 'will') gives the death a formal, conclusive quality — these are closing words, not improvised speech.
detail: The line encodes Brutus's whole tragedy: he killed Caesar reluctantly, 'not for that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more' (3.2), and now he dies willingly, completing the debt. 'Be still' means both 'cease to haunt me' and 'rest in peace.' The couplet form (used for exits and scene-endings throughout Shakespeare) signals finality. The address to Caesar's ghost also closes the play's central dramatic irony: Caesar, physically dead since Act 3, has controlled every subsequent event.

The dual sense of 'be still' (cease to haunt me / rest in peace) is a recognized and uncontroversial reading; the contrast between reluctant killing of Caesar and willing self-death is directly stated by the line's comparative ('not... with half so good a will'), making this an accurate gloss rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: Free from the bondage you are in, Messala: The conquerors can but make a fire of him; For Brutus only overcame himself, And no man else hath honour by his death
summary: Strato's four-line speech turns on a paradox: the victors are enslaved (to ambition, to Fortune), while Brutus, who just died, is free. 'Make a fire of him' means burn his body — the conquerors can only dispose of the corpse, not claim credit for the death. 'Brutus only overcame himself' means no enemy defeated him; his own will was the only force that could.
detail: The phrase 'overcame himself' is a compressed argument about Stoic self-mastery: only a man who is master of himself can choose the moment and manner of his death. Strato's point anticipates and authorizes Antony's eulogy. The language of 'bondage' vs. 'freedom' reverses the political terms of the play: Brutus killed Caesar to prevent Roman enslavement, but Strato now applies those same terms to the victors, who are bound to power and its corruptions. Editors note the speech is likely drawn from Plutarch's account of the aftermath of Philippi ('Life of Brutus,' North 1579, sig. Ppp4v).

Strato's paradox — victors are in bondage, the defeated Brutus is free — is plainly what the lines say; 'make a fire of him' as burning the corpse is the only sense consistent with the conquerors' actual power over the body, and 'overcame himself' as Stoic self-mastery is a mainstream reading well-supported by the context.

anchor_text: So Brutus should be found.--I thank thee, Brutus, That thou hast proved Lucilius' saying true
summary: Lucilius earlier predicted that Brutus would never be taken alive and would die in a manner worthy of him. Now, seeing Brutus dead by his own hand, Lucilius confirms the prediction came true. This is the payoff of the earlier scene (5.4) where Lucilius was captured while impersonating Brutus.

In Plutarch ('Life of Brutus,' North 1579), Lucilius is praised by Antony for his loyalty and kept in his service; Shakespeare follows this. The moment is also a quiet assertion that character is destiny — Brutus died exactly as a man of his type would die.

anchor_text: This was the noblest Roman of them all: All the conspirators, save only he, Did that they did in envy of great Caesar
summary: Antony's eulogy distinguishes Brutus from every other conspirator: the rest acted out of envy or personal grievance, but Brutus genuinely believed he was serving the public good. This is remarkable because Antony is the play's most politically calculating character — for him to grant Brutus this verdict is the play's final judgment on who Brutus was.
detail: The phrase 'noblest Roman' invokes a specific Roman ideal: the vir bonus ('good man'), who places civic virtue above personal advantage. Antony's line 'in a general-honest thought / And common good to all, made one of them' means Brutus joined the conspiracy from general principle rather than private motive. The climax of the speech — 'Nature might stand up / And say to all the world, This was a man' — appeals to the concept of the perfectly balanced human being, composed of the four elements (earth, water, fire, air) in ideal proportion. This is humoral theory: when the elements are 'so mix'd' harmoniously, the result is the complete human. Antony, who stirred the mob against Brutus with theatrical skill in 3.2, here drops the rhetoric and speaks plainly; the contrast underscores the sincerity of the tribute.
